grammarPoint.title: At, on and in for time
grammarPoint.summary: Learn to use 'at' for specific times, 'on' for days and dates, and 'in' for months, seasons, and years.
grammarPoint.explanation:
We use *at* for very specific times. This includes clock times like 'at 7 PM' or 'at noon'. Think of it as a precise point in time.

We use *on* for days of the week and specific dates. For example, 'on Monday' or 'on July 4th'. If you can put 'day' after it, you probably use 'on'.

We use *in* for longer periods of time. This includes months ('in August'), seasons ('in summer'), and years ('in 2023'). We also use 'in' for parts of the day like 'in the morning' or 'in the evening'.
patterns: at + specific time (e.g., at 8 AM, at noon)
on + day of the week (e.g., on Tuesday, on Friday)
on + specific date (e.g., on May 1st, on Christmas Day)
in + month (e.g., in January, in October)
in + season/year/part of day (e.g., in summer, in 2025, in the morning)

examples.text: The store opens at 9 AM every day.
examples.note: Uses 'at' for a specific clock time.

examples.text: I have a meeting on Wednesday.
examples.note: Uses 'on' for a day of the week.

examples.text: We usually go on vacation in the summer.
The new building was finished in 2024.

commonErrors.wrong: I will call you at Friday.
commonErrors.right: I will call you on Friday.
commonErrors.note: Use 'on' for days of the week.

exercises.question: I always go for a walk ___ the morning.
exercises.explanation: Use 'in' for parts of the day like 'the morning'.

exercises.question: Her appointment is ___ Tuesday.
exercises.explanation: Use 'on' for days of the week.

exercises.text: They moved to a new city ___ 2023.
